name: Cornwall
tagline: England's far south-west corner: a rugged coastline of fishing harbours, surf beaches and clifftop paths, with its own language, flag and a claim to being a country apart.
highlight: St Ives' turquoise-watered harbour and beaches, framed by whitewashed cottages and one of Britain's best small art scenes.
shortDescription: A peninsula of dramatic coastline in England's far south-west, mixing fishing harbours, surf beaches, clifftop paths and a distinct Cornish identity.
metaDescription: A Cornwall travel guide: St Ives, the Eden Project, the South West Coast Path, Cornish pasties, when to go and a practical multi-day itinerary.
knownFor: Coastal villages, surf beaches, the Eden Project, pasties

image.alt: St Ives harbour beach with the pier and town beyond

intro: Cornwall occupies England's far south-western tip, a peninsula narrow enough that you're rarely more than half an hour from the sea, and shaped by that coastline more than almost anywhere else in Britain. Fishing has defined its economy and culture for centuries, tin and copper mining before that, and more recently tourism and a thriving food and arts scene.

The identity here runs deeper than scenery. Cornish is a recognised Celtic language with its own revival movement, the black-and-white St Piran's flag flies from houses and cars across the county, and many Cornish people consider Cornwall a distinct nation within the UK rather than simply another English county — worth knowing before referring to it as 'the English seaside'.

The coastline itself does the heavy lifting for visitors: the South West Coast Path runs its entire length, surf beaches line the north coast, sheltered fishing harbours dot the south, and the light — famously drawing artists to St Ives for over a century — has a different quality from the rest of England.

whyVisit.intro: Cornwall's case is that no other part of England combines this much dramatic coastline, distinct culture and excellent food in one accessible region.

points.title: The coastline is spectacular
points.text: Cliffs, coves, surf beaches and fishing harbours change character constantly along a single coast path.

points.title: Cornish identity is real, not marketing
points.text: A distinct language, flag and cultural history give Cornwall a character different from the rest of England.

points.title: The food scene is a genuine national leader
points.text: From Rick Stein's Padstow to countless smaller producers, Cornwall punches well above its weight for British food.

points.title: St Ives' art history is real, not incidental
points.text: The light that drew Turner, Hepworth and generations of artists here still supports a serious gallery scene, Tate St Ives included.

points.title: It rewards both activity and doing nothing
points.text: Surfing, coastal walking and watersports sit alongside beach days and cream tea afternoons, suiting very different kinds of trip.

attractionsIntro: Cornwall is large enough that these are best split across a north-coast and south-coast base rather than rushed as day trips from one town.

attractions.name: St Ives

image.alt: St Ives harbour pier with its lighthouse at low tide

attractions.text: A former fishing harbour turned art town, with turquoise-watered beaches, narrow cobbled streets and Tate St Ives overlooking Porthmeor Beach.
attractions.tip: Park at the Lelant Saltings park-and-ride and take the scenic branch line train in — St Ives' own parking is difficult in summer.

attractions.name: The Eden Project

image.alt: The geodesic biomes of the Eden Project

attractions.text: Two vast geodesic biomes built in a former china clay pit, recreating rainforest and Mediterranean climates, alongside extensive outdoor gardens.
attractions.tip: Allow a full day — the site is considerably larger than it appears from photographs.

attractions.name: St Michael's Mount

image.alt: The castle-topped tidal island of St Michael's Mount

attractions.text: A tidal island crowned by a medieval castle, reachable on foot via a causeway at low tide or by boat when the tide is in.
attractions.tip: Check tide times before visiting — the causeway is only walkable for a few hours around low tide.

attractions.name: Land's End

image.file: File:Granite cliffs at Land's End in Cornwall - geograph.org.uk - 7695015.jpg
image.alt: The granite cliffs of Land's End meeting the Atlantic

attractions.text: The dramatic granite cliffs marking England's most south-westerly point, with striking Atlantic views and a coast path in both directions.
attractions.tip: Skip the commercial attractions at the visitor complex and focus on the cliff walks either side for the real experience.

attractions.name: Tintagel Castle

image.file: File:Tintagel Castle Footbridge by Hufton & Crow.jpg
image.alt: The modern footbridge linking Tintagel Castle's headland to the mainland

attractions.text: Ruined medieval castle ruins on a dramatic headland linked to Arthurian legend, connected to the mainland by a striking modern footbridge.
attractions.tip: The site involves genuine steps and uneven terrain — allow more time than the map distance suggests.

attractions.name: Padstow
attractions.text: A picturesque fishing harbour turned foodie destination, largely thanks to chef Rick Stein, whose restaurants and shops now line the harbourfront.
attractions.tip: The Camel Trail cycle path runs from Padstow along a former railway line, a flat, easy ride through beautiful estuary scenery.

thingsToDoIntro: Beyond the headline sights, Cornwall rewards slower coastal time and a few local activities.

thingsToDo.title: Walk a stretch of the South West Coast Path

image.file: File:South West Coast Path on Carn Moyle Cliff (6834).jpg
image.alt: The South West Coast Path running along a Cornish clifftop

thingsToDo.text: Britain's longest waymarked path runs the entire Cornish coast, with countless manageable day sections offering dramatic cliff and cove scenery.
thingsToDo.tip: The stretch between St Ives and Zennor is among the most scenic and manageable single-day sections.

thingsToDo.title: Learn to surf

image.alt: A surfer riding a wave at Fistral Beach

thingsToDo.text: Cornwall's north coast, particularly around Newquay and Fistral Beach, is Britain's most established surfing region, with schools suited to complete beginners.
thingsToDo.tip: Book a lesson rather than going it alone — Cornish beaches have real rip currents that surf schools know how to navigate safely.

thingsToDo.title: Visit a Cornish pasty shop
thingsToDo.text: A genuine local tradition worth seeking out beyond supermarket versions — small independent bakeries across Cornwall take real pride in the craft.
thingsToDo.tip: A proper Cornish pasty has a crimped edge along the side, not the top — a genuine point of local pride.

thingsToDo.title: Explore a fishing harbour village

image.alt: Fishing boats in the small harbour at Polperro

thingsToDo.text: Beyond the famous names, Cornwall has dozens of smaller harbour villages — Mousehole, Polperro, Port Isaac — worth a wander without a fixed itinerary.
thingsToDo.tip: Port Isaac is instantly recognisable as the filming location for the Doc Martin television series.

thingsToDo.title: Visit a working tin mine

image.alt: The historic Botallack tin mine engine houses on the cliffside

thingsToDo.text: Cornwall's mining heritage, a UNESCO World Heritage site, is preserved at sites like Geevor Tin Mine, with underground tours giving a genuine sense of the industry's history.
thingsToDo.tip: The coastal engine houses near Botallack, used in the Poldark television series, are striking even viewed from the coast path alone.

thingsToDo.title: Visit the Lost Gardens of Heligan

image.file: File:Mud Maid - Lost Gardens of Heligan - Cornwall, England - DSC02646.jpg
image.alt: The Mud Maid sculpture at the Lost Gardens of Heligan

thingsToDo.text: An atmospheric restored Victorian garden, rediscovered overgrown in the 1990s and now one of Britain's most visited gardens.
thingsToDo.tip: The jungle valley and the sleeping giant's head sculpture are the garden's most photographed features.

foodIntro: Cornwall has a strong food identity, from its defining pasty to a food scene punching well above the county's size.

foods.name: Cornish pasty
foods.text: A protected-status pastry of beef, potato, swede and onion, crimped along one edge, originally designed as a portable miners' lunch.
foods.whereToTry: Independent bakeries across Cornwall — genuine local favourites vary town by town.

foods.name: Cornish cream tea

image.alt: Scones with clotted cream and jam, Cornish style

foods.text: Scones with clotted cream and jam, served the Cornish way — jam first, then cream, a genuine and long-running rivalry with Devon's cream-first tradition.
foods.whereToTry: Tearooms throughout Cornwall, with the jam-first order a point of local pride.

foods.name: Fresh seafood

image.file: File:-2019-11-19 Dressed Cromer crab, Garden Street, Cromer.JPG
image.alt: A plate of freshly dressed crab

foods.text: Cornwall's fishing fleets land excellent seafood, crab and mackerel especially, served simply in harbourside restaurants across the county.
foods.whereToTry: Harbourside restaurants in Padstow, St Ives and Newquay, among many others.

foods.name: Cornish ice cream

image.alt: A scoop of Cornish clotted cream ice cream

foods.text: Made with local clotted cream, Cornish ice cream has a genuine reputation across Britain, sold from stalls and shops throughout the county.
foods.whereToTry: Beachside kiosks and dedicated ice cream parlours across Cornwall.

foods.name: Stargazy pie

image.alt: A traditional stargazy pie with fish heads poking through the crust

foods.text: A traditional Cornish pie with fish heads poking through the crust, said to commemorate a fisherman who saved his village from famine, more a curiosity than a daily dish.
foods.whereToTry: Served traditionally around Mousehole's Tom Bawcock's Eve festival in December.

foods.name: Cornish ale and cider
foods.text: A strong local brewing tradition, with Cornish ales and ciders widely available in the county's pubs, several from breweries within a short distance.
foods.whereToTry: Traditional pubs throughout Cornwall, particularly in harbour towns.

accommodation.intro: Cornwall's size means basing yourself in two areas, north and south coast, generally works better than one fixed base.

areas.name: St Ives
areas.bestFor: Art, beaches and the north coast
areas.text: A picturesque base with excellent beaches and galleries, though parking and summer crowds are a real consideration.

areas.name: Padstow or Newquay
areas.text: Padstow suits a food-focused trip; Newquay is the practical base for surfing and a livelier nightlife scene.

areas.name: Falmouth
areas.bestFor: The south coast and Eden Project
areas.text: A genuine working harbour town well placed for the Eden Project, the Lost Gardens of Heligan and the calmer south coast.

gettingThere.intro: Cornwall is far from London — around five hours by car — making rail or a regional flight worth considering.

options.text: Direct trains run from London Paddington to Penzance, around five hours, with stops throughout Cornwall including St Ives via a scenic branch line.
options.detail: The Night Riviera sleeper service offers an overnight option from London to Penzance.

options.text: Cornwall's own airport, with domestic connections to London and other UK cities, cutting the journey considerably compared to driving.
options.detail: A practical option for visitors short on time, avoiding the long drive from other parts of England.

options.text: The most flexible way to explore Cornwall's scattered villages and coastline, though the drive from London takes around five hours.
options.detail: Summer traffic on the A30, Cornwall's main artery, can add significant time on peak weekends.

gettingAround.intro: A car is close to essential for covering Cornwall's spread-out coastline, though branch line trains serve a few key towns well.

options.text: The most practical way to reach Cornwall's scattered villages and beaches, particularly beyond the main towns.
options.detail: Lanes can be narrow in rural areas — allow more time than distances suggest.

options.text: The St Ives Bay Line and other scenic branch lines connect several key towns directly, avoiding Cornwall's summer traffic and limited parking.
options.detail: The St Ives line is considered one of Britain's most scenic short rail journeys.

options.text: For those with time, walking sections of the coast path is a practical way to move between coastal villages.
options.detail: Baggage transfer services exist for those walking multi-day sections without wanting to carry full packs.

bestTime.headline: May–June and September
bestTime.summary: Cornwall's weather is milder than much of Britain, but shoulder months balance good conditions against summer's considerable crowds.

seasons.text: Mild weather, blooming coastal gardens, and crowds well below the summer peak on the main beaches and villages.
The busiest months, with St Ives and Padstow crowded and roads congested, though the best weather and warmest sea for swimming.
Comfortable temperatures, thinning crowds, and often some of the year's best surf as autumn swells arrive.
Quiet and atmospheric, with dramatic storm-watching on the coast, though many smaller attractions and restaurants reduce hours or close.

bestTime.avoid: School summer holiday weeks in late July and August, when Cornwall's roads, car parks and beaches are at their most congested.

itinerary.title: Five days in Cornwall
itinerary.intro: The north coast's art and surf towns first, then south to food and gardens — a loop covering Cornwall's different sides.

days.title: St Ives
days.summary: Settle in and explore the art town's beaches and galleries.
days.morning: Arrive and explore St Ives' harbour and old town.
days.afternoon: Tate St Ives and Porthmeor Beach.

days.title: Land's End and the far west
days.summary: England's most south-westerly point and the mining coast.
days.morning: Drive to Land's End via the coast road.
days.afternoon: The Botallack engine houses and coast path.
days.evening: Return to St Ives or overnight near Penzance.

days.title: St Michael's Mount and the move south
days.summary: A tidal island castle, then relocate toward the south coast.
days.afternoon: Drive toward the Eden Project area.
days.evening: Overnight near St Austell or Falmouth.

days.title: The Eden Project and Heligan
days.morning: The Eden Project's biomes and gardens.

days.title: Padstow and Tintagel
days.summary: Food and Arthurian legend on the way north.
days.morning: Padstow's harbour and a pasty or seafood lunch.

tipsIntro: Practical notes on traffic, tides and timing that make a real difference to a Cornwall trip.
tips: Avoid driving on Saturdays in July and August if possible — changeover day brings Cornwall's worst holiday traffic.
Check tide times before visiting St Michael's Mount — the causeway is only walkable around low tide.
Book Eden Project tickets online in advance for a small discount and to guarantee entry on busy days.
Use park-and-ride or branch line trains for St Ives rather than driving into the town itself.
Order your cream tea Cornish-style — jam first, then cream — if you want to fit in locally.
Book restaurant tables well ahead in Padstow during summer, especially for Rick Stein's establishments.
Pack layers regardless of season — coastal Cornwall's weather can change quickly even in summer.

faq.q: How many days do you need in Cornwall?
faq.a: Four to six. Four covers the essential north-coast towns and one or two major attractions; six allows a proper loop taking in both coasts without feeling rushed.
Largely yes, given how spread out Cornwall's villages and beaches are, though branch line trains cover St Ives and a few other key towns well without one.

faq.q: What is the best time of year to visit?
faq.a: May to June and September offer the best balance of decent weather, long daylight and manageable crowds. Summer is busiest and roads get congested; winter is quiet but many smaller attractions reduce hours.

faq.q: Is Cornwall good for surfing beginners?
faq.a: Yes — Newquay and the wider north coast have well-established surf schools suited to complete beginners, alongside more challenging breaks for experienced surfers.

faq.q: Is Cornwall part of England or somewhere different?
faq.a: Constitutionally part of England, but Cornwall has a distinct Celtic history, its own language and a strong regional identity that many locals consider culturally separate — worth being aware of and respectful toward as a visitor.
